name: Ginkgo biloba

lead: Ginkgo biloba extract comes from the leaves of the ginkgo tree and is one of the best-known herbal supplements for memory and blood flow. People take it for mental performance and general circulation support.

Extracts contain flavonoids and terpene lactones, studied for antioxidant and blood-flow effects. Large reviews have not found conclusive cognitive benefit in healthy people, while a standardised extract is registered in the EU as a herbal medicine for mild dementia.

paras: Used as a daily oral capsule or tablet of standardised leaf extract, often as a background nootropic in recovery or study routines. Users commonly take it for weeks to months.

Reported effects include stomach upset, headache, dizziness and bleeding risk, and interactions with warfarin and antiplatelet drugs are a concern. Ginkgolic acids can cause allergic skin reactions, and many raw seeds can cause ginkgotoxin poisoning. IARC classified the extract as possibly carcinogenic in 2016.

angle.text: Ginkgo is taken for memory and circulation, and users fold it into recovery and study routines for sharper mental performance. Large reviews have not found conclusive cognitive benefit, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

lead: Ginkgo biloba, the ginkgo or maidenhair tree, is a long-lived deciduous tree native to China and the only living species in its division.[1][2] Standardised leaf extracts are sold as supplements and, in some European countries, as herbal medicines for cognitive complaints.[1]

Wikipedia reports use in traditional Chinese medicine since at least the 11th century and states that there is no conclusive evidence for any of its traditional uses.[1] The US NCCIH has said it has never been conclusively proven effective for any condition, while a 2014 European Medicines Agency committee concluded that the leaf extract is effective and safe for improving cognition and quality of life in mild dementia.[1]
Ginkgo has no established role in appearance treatment; it appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent nootropic and "recovery" discussion as a general cognitive and circulation supplement.
infobox: Not an approved drug; sold as supplement

paras: Seeds, nuts and leaves were used in traditional Chinese medicine for dementia, asthma, bronchitis and kidney and bladder disorders.[1] Modern extracts are marketed for memory, circulation and cognition.[2]

Wikipedia summarises recent reviews: a 2023 review found insufficient clinical evidence for therapeutic use; systematic reviews found no benefit for hypertension, menopause-related cognitive problems, tinnitus, post-stroke recovery or altitude sickness; a 2016 systematic review found reduced tardive dyskinesia symptoms in people with schizophrenia; a 2021 umbrella review suggested possible benefit in Alzheimer's disease while a 2023 analysis found insufficient evidence; and a 2026 Cochrane review found little to no meaningful benefit for mild cognitive impairment and low-certainty, small to moderate improvements in dementia symptoms.[1]

A large registered prevention trial enrolled 3,069 older adults to examine dementia and Alzheimer's disease.[3] A trial of ginkgo in mild-to-moderate dementia was also used to measure the Hawthorne effect, comparing minimal and intensive follow-up.[4] Other registered studies have looked at Raynaud's phenomenon[5], glaucoma[6], schizophrenia[7], mild cognitive impairment with cerebrovascular disease[8] and cerebral insufficiency[9]; registry entries describe design, not outcomes.

Wikipedia lists bleeding risk, gastrointestinal upset, headache, dizziness, palpitations and restlessness. Ginkgolic acids and related alkylphenols can cause allergic skin reactions, particularly in people allergic to poison ivy, mango or cashew; large seed intake over time can cause ginkgotoxin poisoning with convulsions.[1] Supplements may affect anticoagulant and antiplatelet drug therapy.[1] A general review of herb-drug interactions also discusses ginkgo among other herbs.[10]

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classified ginkgo extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) in 2016. In 2014 the EMA herbal committee reached the conclusion above for mild dementia. In the United States it is not an approved drug, and the FDA issued warning letters in 2021 to 2023 over false health claims.[1]
